The Moon-toothed degu (Octodon lunatus) is a relatively large-bodied member of the family Octodontidae, with adults attaining an ultimate wet body mass of up to 233 grams [Wwi = up to 233 grams]. Field surveys conducted in the coastal matorral of central Chile suggest that this species exhibits a comparatively slow life-history pace for a rodent of its size. Newborn pups, based on data from the closely related Octodontomys gliroides, are estimated to weigh approximately 17.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 17.5 grams] at birth, a modest neonatal mass that reflects the altricial developmental state typical of octodontid rodents. The gestation period, also inferred from congeneric values, lasts approximately 104 days [tg = approximately 104 days] under standard thermoneutral conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], an extended intrauterine development that is unusual among small mammals and likely contributes to the relatively advanced state of the neonates at parturition. This prolonged gestation is thought to be an adaptation to the energetically demanding environment of the Chilean coastal range.

Following their emergence from the natal burrow, suckling juveniles depend entirely on maternal milk for approximately 92 days after birth [tx = approximately 92 days after birth], a protracted nursing period that is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] and facilitates substantial mass gain prior to the transition to independence. During this suckling stage, the dependent offspring exhibit rapid skeletal growth, supported by the female's sustained lactation effort. The timing of weaning appears to coincide with the onset of the dry season, when the availability of herbaceous forage begins to decline, thereby imposing a strong selective pressure on the mother to wean her litter before resources become limiting. Reproductive output in this species is modest; females typically produce a litter of 2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 pups per litter] and, based on available data from related octodontids, appear capable of approximately 2 reproductive events per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 reproductive events per year]. This relatively low annual reproductive rate is consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy.

Sexual maturation in the Moon-toothed degu is a gradual process that culminates approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This delayed onset of reproductive maturity is typical of rodents that inhabit unpredictable, semi-arid environments, where early breeding may be maladaptive if resource pulses are infrequent. Young animals undergo a prolonged juvenile phase during which they refine foraging skills and establish social hierarchies before entering the breeding population. Males are thought to reach testicular maturity later than females, though precise data on the timing of first spermatogenesis remain scarce for wild populations. The extended pre-reproductive period may also serve to reduce intraspecific competition for breeding territories, as suitable burrow sites in the degraded coastal scrub are limited.

Respirometry trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have quantified the resting metabolism of Octodon lunatus. At a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate measured in post-absorptive adults reaches 171.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 171.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This elevated oxygen consumption is notably high for a rodent of 233 grams [Wwi = 233 grams] and likely reflects the energetic demands of thermoregulation in the cool, fog-inundated habitats that this species occupies at higher elevations. The metabolic measurements were obtained from individuals acclimated to captive conditions for several weeks, ensuring that stress-induced hypermetabolism was minimized. Compared to the Chilean degu (Octodon degus), the Moon-toothed degu appears to exhibit a slightly higher mass-specific metabolic rate, a finding that warrants further investigation into potential differences in thyroid hormone activity and mitochondrial efficiency between these two congeners.

Longevity records for the Moon-toothed degu, while limited, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] under captive conditions at a maintained body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, which is several times longer than that predicted by allometric equations for a rodent of its ultimate wet body mass of 233 grams [Wwi = 233 grams], is a hallmark of the slow life-history syndrome observed in members of the family Octodontidae. The physiological mechanisms underlying this exceptional longevity are poorly understood but may involve enhanced resistance to oxidative stress and delayed reproductive senescence. In the wild, mortality is likely highest among dispersing juveniles and during periods of extreme drought, when food resources become scarce and predation pressure from foxes and raptors intensifies. The combination of a protracted gestation, slow sexual maturation, extended lifespan, and modest annual reproductive output clearly positions Octodon lunatus as a species with a strongly conservative life-history strategy.
